member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioCVars
member.summary: The audio system's console variables.

remarks.para: Declared next to the audio seam, the way the renderer declares its own. The console, the settings file and the options menu all reach these through , so there is one value and three views onto it. The snd_ prefix is the one the settings screen already builds its Audio page from — until this file existed, that page rendered empty.

The volumes here are the output side. They are distinct from the player profile's own sound settings, which the original stores per profile and which remain the value the game's own menus edit; the profile feeds these, not the other way round.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioCVars.Preset
member.summary: Which named profile the audio settings correspond to.

remarks.para: Setting this writes the profile's values over the variables it names, which is how -vanilla reaches the audio system: the flag emits snd_preset vanilla as a start-up statement, exactly as it emits gfx_preset vanilla for the renderer.

It has to be set before the device opens to take full effect. The voice count and the output rate are read once, when the device is created; the panning model is read per voice and so does follow a change immediately.

member.summary: The gain of the rain bed, over and above the ambience bus.
member.remarks: Separate from because they answer different questions: the bus says how loud the level's beds are against the gunfire, and this says how loud the rain is against the rest of the beds. A player who wants a quieter storm and the same generators wants this one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioCVars.RainWallLevel
member.summary: How much of the rain outside a wall is heard through it, as an amplitude.

remarks.para: The floor under the whole indoor mix, and the number that decides whether stepping inside sounds like shelter or like a cellar. It has to carry the interior on its own wherever the roof is too high to drum — a warehouse, a hangar, anything with a ceiling out of reach — because there the drumming contributes nothing and this is all that is left.

Thirteen decibels down. Genuine transmission loss through a solid wall is rather more than that, but the buildings in this game are sheds, huts and light industrial shells, and a storm you can barely hear from inside one reads as a bug rather than as insulation.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioCVars.RainWallCutoffHz
member.summary: The cutoff the through-the-wall component is heard through, in hertz.
member.remarks: Rain's own energy peaks between one and two and a half kilohertz, so a cutoff below that takes the rain out of the rain and leaves a rumble that could be anything. Just under a kilohertz keeps enough of the peak for it to still be recognisable through the wall.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioCVars.RainRoofLevel

member.remarks: Well above the walls: a roof is thin, it is struck directly by the drops, and it is the sound that makes a shed in a storm unmistakably a shed in a storm.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioCVars.RainDebug

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioListenerState
member.summary: Where the listener is and which way it faces.

remarks.para: Positions are in metres and are , matching the rest of the port: world positions are double throughout, and the render world divides raw engine units by 4096 on load. A caller holding engine units must divide by UnitsPerMetre before it gets here.

The orientation is the engine's own eye basis, whose columns are right, forward and up — the frame sub_4B38E0 composes and the AI vision cone is measured in. It is applied with the engine's v · M convention, which is what does; using the other convention transposes the rotation and mirrors the stereo image.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioListenerState.FromViewRotation(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f)
member.summary: Builds a listener from a camera's world-to-view rotation.
member.param: Where the ear is, in metres.
A world-to-view rotation whose rows are the view axes in the order right, up, forward — the shape Camera3D.LookRotation returns.
member.returns: A listener whose orientation is the engine eye basis this type expects.

remarks.para: These are two different matrices and confusing them is silent, not loud. A camera's world-to-view rotation carries its axes in its rows, in the order right, up, forward; the engine's eye basis carries them in its columns, in the order right, forward, up. Handing the first straight to reads column 2 as forward when column 2 is not even an axis of the frame — at an unrotated pose it yields forward +Z and up +Y, so the listener faces straight up.

What that sounds like is a source above the player arriving dead ahead: centred, unpanned and seemingly right on top of the listener however far away it really is. Transposing moves the rows into the columns; the swap puts forward ahead of up.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.AudioVolumeCurve
member.summary: The original's gain curve — the table Snd_Init builds before it touches DirectSound, and the thing that makes the game's volume sliders feel the way they do.

remarks.para: 0x4952F0 fills 10001 entries at 0x67A4A0, indexed by gain × 10000. Each entry is trunc(ln(gain) × 1442.695040888849), clamped to [−10000, 0], written backwards from the last entry down; entry zero is stored as the floor before the loop rather than computed.

The unit is not decibels, and that is the interesting part. The constant is 1000 / ln(2), so the entry is 1000 × log2(gain) — one thousand units per halving. The value is then handed straight to IDirectSoundBuffer::SetVolume, which reads it as hundredths of a decibel. A halving therefore attenuates by 10 dB where true amplitude decibels would give 6.02, so the original's curve is about 1.66× steeper than a dB curve. Sounds fall away faster than a straight port of "gain to dB" would make them, and a mix built on the arithmetically correct curve is audibly wrong. The floor, −10000, is reached at a gain of 2^−10 ≈ 0.00098.

It matters that this is a table and not a formula: the original quantises the gain to one of 10001 steps before taking the logarithm, so two gains differing in the fifth decimal produce exactly the same attenuation. Reproducing the quantisation is what makes the vanilla profile match rather than merely resemble.
The curve is also how a pan becomes an attenuation: the original puts 1 − |pan| through the same table and signs the result.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.FilteredLoopSource
member.summary: One tap on a shared, endlessly looping block of mono PCM, low-passed by an amount the game moves while the tap is sounding.

remarks.para: This exists for the continuous beds — rain above all — where the same recording has to be heard from several directions at once and each direction has to sound like the path it took to get here. Rain arriving through an open door is the recording; the same rain arriving through the wall beside it is the recording with its top three octaves gone. A resident buffer cannot express that, because the device offers gain and pitch and nothing else, so the filtering is done here, on the samples, as they are pulled.

The PCM is shared and never copied. Every tap holds the same and only its own read cursor, so a two-megabyte loop costs two megabytes however many directions are sounding. Giving each tap a different starting frame is what keeps them from being the same signal six times over: six copies of one waveform sum coherently and collapse to a point between the speakers, where six different stretches of the same rain sum incoherently and stay spread out.

The cutoff is smoothed towards its target rather than assigned. A filter coefficient stepped once a frame is a click once a frame; approached over a fifth of a second it is a door opening. Because the smoothing runs per sample inside , a caller may set as often as it likes and never hear the individual steps.

Latency. A gain change reaches the ear at once, because gain belongs to the device's own source; a cutoff change reaches it only when the buffers already queued ahead of it have played, which is a quarter of a second at the device's default queue depth. That is the right way round: level is what a listener notices being late, and a doorway takes longer than a quarter second to walk through in any case.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Audio.FilteredLoopSource.OpenCutoffHz
member.summary: The cutoff that means "do not filter at all", in hertz.
member.remarks: At or above the sample rate's Nyquist frequency the coefficient is exactly zero and both poles pass their input through unchanged, so an outdoor tap is bit-for-bit the recording rather than the recording through a filter that is merely wide. Callers blending towards "open" should blend towards this value.

member.remarks: Below this the bed stops being muffled rain and starts being a hum with no rain in it at all. Concrete and rain together do not get duller than this in life either.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.IAudioDevice
member.summary: The seam between the game and whatever is making noise — the audio counterpart of IGraphicsDevice.

remarks.para: OpenIGI.Engine and OpenIGI.Game talk to this and never to a backend. The backend is chosen in the composition root — OpenAL in apps/OpenIGI.Desktop, the Web Audio API in apps/OpenIGI.Web — exactly as the renderer is.

The model is the original's, generalised only where it had to be. There is a fixed pool of voices — the original allocates 32 of 76 bytes each in Snd_Init 0x4952F0 — and a request that finds none free either steals a less important one or is dropped. Buffers are shared, so the same sound backs any number of voices at once.
Everything here is called from the game thread. A device that needs a worker of its own — a streaming pump, for instance — owns it privately and must not call back into game code.

A device is always usable. When no hardware can be opened, the implementation degrades to silence rather than throwing: goes and every call still succeeds. A machine with no sound card must boot, play and pass its tests.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.VanillaSpatialiser
member.summary: The original's positional audio, exactly as it computed it: a linear distance rolloff and a pan, folded into the gain and balance of an otherwise flat stereo voice.

remarks.para: Transcribed from the voice update 0x496E60. The original is not DirectSound3D. Its primary buffer is created with flags 0x9 and its sample buffers with 0x100E8 — neither carries DSBCAPS_CTRL3D. Every sound in the game is a mono or stereo buffer whose apparent position is hand-computed into volume, pan and playback frequency, three times a tick. This class is that computation, and it is what the vanilla profile uses instead of letting OpenAL position anything.
Two details of it are worth stating because they are not what a modern engine would do:

item.description: The distance rolloff is linear between the two distances, not inverse-square and not inverse-clamped. A source is at full gain inside the minimum distance, fades on a straight line to silence at the maximum, and is cut entirely beyond it.

The pan is localX / (minimum + maximum) — the lateral offset over the sum of the two distances. Distance cancels out of it entirely, so a source ten metres to the left pans exactly as hard whether it is ten metres away or fifty. It is not a direction; it is a lateral offset measured against a fixed scale.

member.summary: Everything the device needs to know about one playing sound.

remarks.para: Distances are in metres, matching . The original stores them in metres too and multiplies by 4096 in the voice update to compare against engine-unit positions; keeping both sides in metres removes the conversion without changing any ratio, because every use of the two distances in 0x496E60 is a ratio.

A voice is either positional or not. A positional voice takes and the two distances and has its gain and pan derived; a flat one takes as given. The original draws the same line with two flag bits on the voice record — 0x2 selects positional and 0x4 suppresses panning altogether.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Audio.VoicePool`1
member.summary: A device's fixed pool of voices: allocation, stealing, handles and stream refills.

remarks.para: The model is the original's — a fixed number of voices allocated once (Snd_Init 0x4952F0 makes 32) and reused for the life of the device — with the bookkeeping every backend needs done once here: which slots are free, which to steal, what a handle encodes, and how a stream is refilled. A backend supplies the two things only it knows: how to make a slot of its own kind and how to silence one.
A handle packs the slot index and its generation, so a handle to a voice that has since been stolen resolves to nothing rather than to whatever took its place.
Not thread-safe. The device that owns the pool is called from the game thread only, and keeps its own lock where it wants one.
